context: Exam set 2. Let $p$ and $q$ both have highest power $x^n$ with leading coefficients $a$ and $b$ satisfying $a+b=0$ and $a\neq 0$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The highest power of $x$ in $p+q$ is strictly less than $n$.
The highest power of $x$ in $p-q$ is still $x^{n}$.
The highest power of $x$ in $p\cdot q$ is $x^{2n}$.
$p$ and $-q$ share the same leading coefficient.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Opposite leading coefficients cancel the top power of the sum, dropping the highest remaining exponent strictly below $n$.

$$p(x)=x^{2}+1$$

together with

$$q(x)=-x^{2}+x$$

$$p(x)+q(x)=x+1$$

Here $n=2$ and

$$a+b=1+(-1)$$

$$a+b=0$$

, so the $x^{2}$ terms cancel and the sum has highest power $x^{1}$. In general the coefficient of $x^{n}$ in $p+q$ is $a+b=0$. The highest power of $p+q$ is strictly less than $n$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Subtracting reverses the sign of $b$, so the top coefficients no longer cancel: they double.

$$p(x)-q(x)=\bigl(x^{2}+1\bigr)-\bigl(-x^{2}+x\bigr)$$

$$p(x)-q(x)=2x^{2}-x+1$$

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

The leading coefficient is $a-b=a-(-a)=2a\neq 0$, since $a\neq 0$. In the example the top term is $2x^{2}$, so the highest power of $p-q$ remains $x^{n}$ with $n=2$. Subtracting cannot cancel opposite leads.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Cancellation of the leading terms does not force every lower coefficient to vanish, so $p+q$ need not be the zero polynomial.

$$p(x)+q(x)=x+1$$

That sum is linear, not identically zero. A second pair $x^{n}$ and $-x^{n}+1$ likewise leaves the constant $1$.

$$x^{n}+(-x^{n}+1)=1$$

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

Only the top power is guaranteed to disappear, so $p+q$ is not forced to be the zero polynomial.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Leading coefficients multiply, and

$$ab=a(-a)$$

$$ab=-a^{2}$$

 is nonzero because $a\neq 0$.

$$p(x)q(x)=(x^{2}+1)(-x^{2}+x)$$

$$p(x)q(x)=-x^{4}+x^{3}-x^{2}+x$$

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

A nonzero coefficient of that highest power is what makes the degree exact.

The top power is $x^{4}=x^{2n}$. In general the product of two degree-$n$ polynomials with nonzero leads has highest power $x^{2n}$. The product keeps $x^{2n}$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

The leading coefficient of $-q$ is $-b$, and the hypothesis $a+b=0$ rewrites as $-b=a$.

$$-q(x)=x^{2}-x$$

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

That leading coefficient is $1$, which is exactly the leading coefficient $a$ of $p(x)=x^{2}+1$. In general $-q$ starts with $-b\,x^{n}=a\,x^{n}$, the same top term as $p$. So $p$ and $-q$ share the leading coefficient $a$.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
Everything is stated for a general polynomial, so the reasoning runs on highest powers, parity, and the factor theorem instead of on a single numerical example.

Opposite leading coefficients remove the top power in $p+q$.

Degree and the leading coefficient are read from the highest written power whose coefficient is not zero.

The factor theorem is a substitution: $x-r$ divides a polynomial if and only if the value at $r$ is zero.

title: Parameter t: How Many Real Zeros?
context:
Let $g_k(x)=x^3-kx$ with real $k$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.

(Exam variant 85.)
statements: If $k>0$, then $g_k$ has three distinct real zeros.
If $k=0$, then $g_k$ has three distinct real zeros.
If $k<0$, then $g_k$ has only one real zero.
The leading coefficient of $g_k$ depends on $k$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Factor out $x$ and read the remaining quadratic: three distinct real zeros appear precisely when that quadratic has two nonzero real roots.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{k}(x)=x(x^{2}-k)$$

Take $k=4>0$. Then $x^{2}=4$, so the zeros are $-2$, $0$ and $2$.

$$g_{4}(x)=x(x-2)(x+2)$$

Distinct zeros ignore multiplicity: a squared factor still counts as one abscissa.

Those three numbers are distinct. The same pattern $0,\pm\sqrt{k}$ holds for every $k>0$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Setting the parameter to zero collapses the family to a pure cube, which has only one distinct real zero.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{0}(x)=x^{3}-0\cdot x$$

$$x^{3}-0\cdot x=x^{3}$$

$$x^{3}=0$$

The only real solution is $x=0$, now of multiplicity three. Three distinct zeros would need three different numbers, and a triple root at the origin is just one number. The case $k=0$ fails the count.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

A negative parameter makes $x^{2}-k$ a sum of squares, hence always positive, so the factorisation leaves only the root $x=0$.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{k}(x)=x(x^{2}-k)$$

For $k=-4$ this is $x(x^{2}+4)$, and $x^{2}+4\ge 4>0$ for every real $x$.

$$x^{2}+4=0$$

has no real solution. The only real zero is $x=0$, so a negative $k$ leaves a single real zero.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The leading coefficient is the number in front of $x^{3}$, and that number is written as $1$ for every member of the family.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{k}(x)=x^{3}-kx$$

$$g_{1}(x)=x^{3}-x$$

and

$$g_{5}(x)=x^{3}-5x$$

Both start with $x^{3}$. The parameter $k$ only rescales the linear term; it never touches the cubic coefficient. The leading coefficient is constantly $1$, independent of $k$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Oddness is the identity $g_{k}(-x)=-g_{k}(x)$, and both terms of the family carry odd powers of $x$.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{k}(-x)=(-x)^{3}-k(-x)$$

$$g_{k}(-x)=-x^{3}+kx$$

$$g_{k}(-x)=-(x^{3}-kx)$$

$$-(x^{3}-kx)=-g_{k}(x)$$

Equivalently, every surviving power in the expansion must be odd.

The parameter $k$ rides along untouched, so the identity holds for every real $k$, including $k=0$. The family is odd for every real $k$.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
The family is given explicitly, with the parameter sitting on a lower term, so the leading term never sees it.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g(x)=x \left(- k + x^{2}\right)$$

Factor $x(x^{2}-k)$ to read the root count from the sign of $k$.

Degree and the leading coefficient are read from the highest written power whose coefficient is not zero.

Parity is a coefficient reading: only odd powers make an odd map, only even powers make an even map.

title: Negative Leading Coefficient Cubic
context: The figure shows a cubic with leading coefficient $-1$ and zeros $-2$, $0$ and $3$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The product of the zeros equals $0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The right-hand end of a cubic is settled by the leading term $-x^{3}$, which the figure names explicitly.

$$p(x)=-x(x+2)(x-3)$$

$$p(x)=-x^{3}+x^{2}+6x$$

For large positive $x$ the cubic term dominates, and $-x^{3}$ is large and negative.

$$\lim_{x\to+\infty}p(x)=-\infty$$

Odd degree with a negative lead therefore dives on the far right.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The origin is listed as a zero, which is the statement that the graph meets the axis at $x=0$.

$$p(x)=-x(x+2)(x-3)$$

$$p(0)=0\cdot(-2)\cdot(-3)$$

$$0\cdot -2=0$$

$$0\cdot -3=0$$

$$p(0)=0$$

$$0\cdot(-2)\cdot(-3)$$

The same number is the constant term of the expanded formula.

The explicit factor $-x$ vanishes at the origin, so the product is zero regardless of the other two roots. The expanded form $-0+0+0=0$ agrees. The intercept is $0$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Three distinct real zeros place one stationary point in each gap, and a cubic cannot have more than two.

$$p'(x)=-3x^{2}+2x+6$$

$$2^{2}-4(-3)(6)$$

$$p'(x)=76$$

The discriminant is positive, so $p'$ has two distinct real roots. Rolle's theorem already puts one of them in $(-2,0)$ and the other in $(0,3)$. Two turning points occur.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

A strict inequality $p(0)>0$ needs a positive intercept, but $0$ is itself a listed zero.

$$p(x)=-x(x+2)(x-3)$$

$$p(0)=0$$

The same number is the constant term of the expanded formula.

The graph passes through the origin rather than sitting above it. Expanding $p(x)=-x^{3}+x^{2}+6x$ shows the constant term is $0$, so the intercept is not positive. The number $0$ is not greater than $0$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The three zeros named on the figure are $-2$, $0$ and $3$, and any product that includes $0$ is $0$.

$$
(-2)\cdot 0\cdot 3 =0
$$

The expanded rule $p(x)=-x^{3}+x^{2}+6x$ has constant term $0$, matching that product. Vieta for a cubic $-x^{3}+\cdots$ ties the constant term to the signed product of the zeros, here $0$. The product of the zeros is $0$.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
The figure prints no expanded formula, so the polynomial is recovered from the ticks: zeros, intercept, and the far-field sign.

$p(x)=-x \left(x^{2} - x - 6\right)$.

A value is obtained by substituting the named number and collecting powers.

The factor theorem is a substitution: $x-r$ divides a polynomial if and only if the value at $r$ is zero.

title: Quartic Minus a Parabola
context: Let $p(x)=x^{4} - 5 x^{2} + 4$ and $\ell(x)=x^{2} - 1$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The graphs meet at least twice on the real line.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Meetings solve $p-\ell=0$, so subtract and factor the resulting even quartic as a quadratic in $x^{2}$.

$$p(x)=x^{4} - 5 x^{2} + 4$$

$$p(x)-\ell(x)=x^{4}-5x^{2}+4-(x^{2}-1)$$

$$p(x)-\ell(x)=x^{4}-6x^{2}+5$$

$$(x^{2}-1)(x^{2}-5)=0$$

The real solutions are $x=\pm 1$ and $x=\pm\sqrt{5}$, four distinct meetings. That is certainly at least two.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The highest power of $p-\ell$ is the highest power that does not cancel, and both $p$ and $\ell$ are even.

$$p(x)-\ell(x)=x^{4}-6x^{2}+5$$

The $x^{4}$ term of $p$ has no counterpart in $\ell$, so it survives.

$$x^{4}$$

Evenness requires the expanded formula to survive $x\mapsto -x$.

$$p(-x)=p(x)$$

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

A polynomial whose top power is $x^{4}$ is quartic, not cubic. The $x^{3}$ coefficient in $p-\ell$ is $0$ as well, so the cubic label has nothing to attach to.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Evenness is the identity $p(-x)=p(x)$, and every exponent in $p$ is even.

$$p(x)=x^{4} - 5 x^{2} + 4$$

$$p(-x)=(-x)^{4}-5(-x)^{2}+4$$

$$p(-x)=x^{4}-5x^{2}+4$$

$$p(-x)=p(x)$$

Equivalently, every surviving power in the expansion must be even.

Substituting $-x$ leaves the formula unchanged. A numerical check

$$p(2)=16-20+4$$

$$p(2)=0$$

$$p(2)=p(-2)$$

 agrees, as does

$$p(1)=1-5+4$$

$$p(1)=0$$

$$p(1)=p(-1)$$

. The graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

A linear function has highest power $x^{1}$, so inspect the written rule for $\ell$.

$$p(x)=x^{4} - 5 x^{2} + 4$$

$$\ell(x)=x^{2}-1$$

The top term is $x^{2}$, with leading coefficient $1$.

$$x^{2}$$

That is a quadratic, not a line. The graph of $\ell$ is a parabola: $\ell(0)=-1$ and $\ell(2)=3$ already fail to sit on a line of slope matching a single power $x$. The highest power is $x^{2}$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Compare the two constant terms, which are the heights at $x=0$.

$$p(0)=4$$

$$\ell(0)=-1$$

$$4=-1$$

The same number is the constant term of the expanded formula.

The quartic sits four units above the origin while the parabola sits one unit below it. A meeting at $x=0$ would require $p(0)=\ell(0)$, that is $4=-1$, which is false. Those two constant terms differ exactly.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
The stem names the polynomial that every later computation refers to.

$$p(x)=x^{4} - 5 x^{2} + 4$$

Meetings solve $p-\ell=0$, i.e. $x^{4} - 6 x^{2} + 5=0$.

A value is obtained by substituting the named number and collecting powers.

Parity is a coefficient reading: only odd powers make an odd map, only even powers make an even map.

title: H: Tank Height
context: A model gives $H(t)=\frac{t \left(t^{2} - 50 t + 200\right)}{200}$ for $t\ge 0$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The highest power of $t$ in $H$ is $t^{3}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

The model is rising at a named time only if $H'$ is positive there, so expand and differentiate.

$$H(t)=\frac{t^{3}-50t^{2}+200t}{200}$$

$$H'(t)=\frac{3t^{2}-100t+200}{200}$$

$$H'(12)=\frac{432-1200+200}{200}$$

$$H'(12)=\frac{-71}{25}$$

The value $-\frac{71}{25}$ is negative, so the tank is falling at $t=12$ rather than rising.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Substitute $t=12$ into the factored model and simplify the fraction.

$$H(12)=\frac{12\bigl(144-600+200\bigr)}{200}$$

$$H(12)=\frac{12\cdot(-256)}{200}$$

$$H(12)=\frac{-3072}{200}$$

$$H(12)=-\frac{384}{25}$$

The exact height is the quoted value. As a decimal that is $-15.36$, matching $-384\div 25$. The substitution agrees with the claim.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Distribute the constant $200$ and read the largest surviving exponent.

$$H(t)=\frac{1}{200}t^{3}-\frac{1}{4}t^{2}+t$$

The coefficient of $t^{3}$ is $\frac{1}{200}\neq 0$, so that term is present.

$$t^{3}$$

No higher power appears, and the cubic term survives. Multiplying through by $200$ recovers the numerator $t^{3}-50t^{2}+200t$, whose top power is visibly $t^{3}$. The highest power of $t$ in $H$ is $t^{3}$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

The model has an explicit factor of $t$, so the intercept at the opening instant is zero.

$$H(t)=\frac{t(t^{2}-50t+200)}{200}$$

$$H(0)=\frac{0\cdot 200}{200}$$

$$H(0)=0$$

The factor test is the substitution that asks whether the height vanishes at that abscissa.

With no elapsed time the predicted height relative to the datum is zero. Expanding $H(t)=\frac{1}{200}t^{3}-\frac{1}{4}t^{2}+t$ shows there is no constant term, so $H(0)=0$ identically. The value is $0$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

A quadratic function would have highest power $t^{2}$ and nothing above it, so look at the expanded rule.

$$H(t)=\frac{1}{200}t^{3}-\frac{1}{4}t^{2}+t$$

The cubic term is present with a nonzero coefficient.

$$\frac{1}{200}t^{3}$$

A model whose top power is $t^{3}$ is cubic rather than quadratic. If $H$ were quadratic the $t^{3}$ coefficient would have to be $0$, but $\frac{1}{200}\neq 0$. The quadratic label fails.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
The model is a named polynomial of time, quantity, or cost; later claims are substitutions, derivatives, or tabled increments.

Differentiate $H$ and evaluate at the named input.

Degree and the leading coefficient are read from the highest written power whose coefficient is not zero.

title: Finite Differences Diagnose the Degree (Set 3)
context: Sample set 3: a polynomial $p$ is tabulated below. Evaluate each statements. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The column at $x=1$ lists the height $1$, and the proposed cubic returns the same number.

$$p(1)=1$$

$$1^{3}-1+1$$

Both the table and the closed form agree on $1$. The neighbouring columns $p(0)=1$ and $p(2)=7$ sit on either side of this height, consistent with a cubic that is flat-then-rising. The value at $x=1$ is the number named.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

On equally spaced samples the first differences are neighbouring heights subtracted in order.

$$1,1,7,25$$

The order-1 differences of $1,1,7,25$ are

$$
1-1 =0
$$

$$
7-1 =6
$$

$$
25-7 =18
$$

The resulting row is $0,6,18$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

The column at $x=3$ lists $25$, and substituting into the proposed cubic reproduces that entry.

$$p(3)=25$$

$$27-3=24$$

$$24+1=25$$

$$p(3)=25$$

The table and $x^{3}-x+1$ agree on $25$. The previous column $p(2)=7$ and the first-difference jump $18$ already show the cubic acceleration into this last listed height. The named height is correct.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Test the cubic $x^{3}-x+1$ against every listed column, not just one of them.

$$
0^{3}-0+1 =1
$$

$$8-2=6$$

$$
6+1=7 =7
$$

$$27-3=24$$

$$
24+1=25 =25
$$

The remaining column $x=1$ returns $1$ as well. First differences $0,6,18$ already grow, matching a cubic rather than a line or a parabola. Every tabulated height matches $x^{3}-x+1$ exactly.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Four samples of a line would need constant first differences, but these jumps already grow, and the third differences of a cubic are the ones that settle.

$$0,\ 6,\ 18$$

$$6,\ 12$$

The second differences still move, which already rules out both a line and a parabola. The closed form $x^{3}-x+1$ is cubic. The samples are not linear.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
The table is the whole stem: raw equally spaced samples, with no difference columns printed.

Values match $x^{3} - x + 1$.

A value is obtained by substituting the named number and collecting powers.

On equally spaced samples, a frozen difference layer diagnoses the degree.

title: Parameter α1: How Many Real Zeros?
context:
Let $g_k(x)=x^3-kx$ with real $k$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.

(Exam variant 90.)
statements: If $k>0$, then $g_k$ has three distinct real zeros.
If $k=0$, then $g_k$ has three distinct real zeros.
If $k<0$, then $g_k$ has only one real zero.
The leading coefficient of $g_k$ depends on $k$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

For a positive parameter the quadratic factor $x^{2}-k$ has two real roots, distinct from each other and from $0$.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{k}(x)=x(x^{2}-k)$$

With $k=9$ those roots are $\pm 3$, so the zero set is $\{-3,0,3\}$.

$$g_{9}(3)=27-27$$

$$27-27$$

$$g_{9}(3)=0$$

Distinct zeros ignore multiplicity: a squared factor still counts as one abscissa.

Three different real numbers, and the same counting $0,\pm\sqrt{k}$ works for every $k>0$. Three distinct real zeros occur.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The zero-parameter member of the family is a monomial cube, whose only real root is the origin.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{0}(x)=x^{3}$$

$$g_{0}(x)=x\cdot x\cdot x$$

Distinct zeros ignore multiplicity: a squared factor still counts as one abscissa.

That is a single distinct zero of multiplicity three, not three different axis crossings. For instance $g_{0}(1)=1\neq 0$ and $g_{0}(-1)=-1\neq 0$. Distinctness fails as soon as $k=0$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

When $k$ is negative the quadratic $x^{2}-k$ never hits zero, because it equals $x^{2}$ plus a positive constant.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{-1}(x)=x^{3}+x$$

$$x^{3}+x=x(x^{2}+1)$$

$$x^{2}+1\ge 1>0$$

The only real solution of $x(x^{2}+1)=0$ is $x=0$. A second sample $k=-4$ gives $x(x^{2}+4)$, again only $x=0$. Every negative $k$ leaves this same single real zero.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Write two members side by side and compare the coefficients of $x^{3}$.

$$g_{2}(x)=x^{3}-2x$$

$$g_{7}(x)=x^{3}-7x$$

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

A nonzero coefficient of that highest power is what makes the degree exact.

Both are monic cubics: the number in front of $x^{3}$ is $1$ in each case. Changing $k$ only changes the coefficient of $x$, from $-2$ to $-7$ in the sample. The leading coefficient does not depend on $k$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Every power in $x^{3}-kx$ is odd, so replacing $x$ by $-x$ multiplies the whole formula by $-1$.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{k}(-x)=-x^{3}+kx$$

$$-g_{k}(x)=-x^{3}+kx$$

Equivalently, every surviving power in the expansion must be odd.

The two sides match for every real $k$. In particular

$$g_{0}(-x)=-x^{3}$$

$$g_{0}(-x)=-g_{0}(x)$$

 still holds, and

$$g_{1}(-2)=-8+2$$

$$g_{1}(-2)=-6$$

$$g_{1}(-2)=-g_{1}(2)$$

. The family is odd for every real $k$.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
The family is given explicitly, with the parameter sitting on a lower term, so the leading term never sees it.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g(x)=x \left(- k + x^{2}\right)$$

Factor $x(x^{2}-k)$ to read the root count from the sign of $k$.

Degree and the leading coefficient are read from the highest written power whose coefficient is not zero.

Parity is a coefficient reading: only odd powers make an odd map, only even powers make an even map.

title: Parameter α2: How Many Real Zeros?
context:
Let $g_k(x)=x^3-kx$ with real $k$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.

(Exam variant 91.)
statements: If $k>0$, then $g_k$ has three distinct real zeros.
If $k=0$, then $g_k$ has three distinct real zeros.
If $k<0$, then $g_k$ has only one real zero.
The leading coefficient of $g_k$ depends on $k$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Solve $x^{3}-kx=0$ by factoring, then use the sign of $k$ to count the real roots of $x^{2}=k$.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$x(x^{2}-k)=0$$

If $k>0$ then $x=0$ together with $x=\pm\sqrt{k}$ are three different real numbers. For $k=1$ this is the familiar $x(x-1)(x+1)$.

$$g_{1}(x)=x^{3}-x$$

Distinct zeros ignore multiplicity: a squared factor still counts as one abscissa.

Three distinct real zeros occur whenever $k$ is positive.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Plug $k=0$ into the same factorisation: the quadratic factor becomes $x^{2}$, and the three roots collide.

$$g_{0}(x)=x^{3}$$

$$x^{3}=x\cdot x\cdot x$$

$$x=0$$

Only one distinct real zero remains, of multiplicity three. Nearby values $g_{0}(1)=1$ and $g_{0}(-1)=-1$ are nonzero, so no extra axis crossings hide off the origin. The claim that three distinct zeros survive at $k=0$ is therefore wrong.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

A negative $k$ turns $x^{2}-k$ into a positive-definite quadratic, so it contributes no extra real root.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{-9}(x)=x^{3}+9x$$

$$x^{3}+9x=x(x^{2}+9)$$

$$x^{2}+9=0$$

has no real solution, because $x^{2}+9\ge 9$. The factor $x$ still gives the simple root $x=0$, and nothing else. A nearby value $g_{-9}(1)=1+9=10\neq 0$ confirms there is no extra real zero. Only one real zero remains.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The cubic term is written without a parameter in front of it, so the lead cannot move with $k$.

$$g_{k}(x)=1\cdot x^{3}-k\cdot x$$

Compare $k=0$ and $k=10$: both formulas begin with $x^{3}$.

$$g_{0}(x)=x^{3}$$

and

$$g_{10}(x)=x^{3}-10x$$

A nonzero coefficient of that highest power is what makes the degree exact.

The leading coefficient is $1$ in every case. It does not depend on $k$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Test the odd identity directly on the two-term formula, keeping $k$ as a spectator.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{k}(-x)=(-x)^{3}-k(-x)$$

$$(-x)^{3}-k(-x)=-x^{3}+kx$$

$$g_{k}(-x)=-(x^{3}-kx)$$

$$-(x^{3}-kx)=-g_{k}(x)$$

The algebra never uses the sign or the size of $k$, so the identity is valid for every real parameter. A check at $k=2$:

$$g_{2}(-1)=-1+2$$

$$g_{2}(-1)=1$$

 and

$$-g_{2}(1)=-(1-2)$$

$$-g_{2}(1)=1$$

. Each $g_{k}$ is an odd function.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
The family is given explicitly, with the parameter sitting on a lower term, so the leading term never sees it.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g(x)=x \left(- k + x^{2}\right)$$

Factor $x(x^{2}-k)$ to read the root count from the sign of $k$.

Degree and the leading coefficient are read from the highest written power whose coefficient is not zero.

Parity is a coefficient reading: only odd powers make an odd map, only even powers make an even map.

title: Parameter α3: How Many Real Zeros?
context:
Let $g_k(x)=x^3-kx$ with real $k$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.

(Exam variant 92.)
statements: If $k>0$, then $g_k$ has three distinct real zeros.
If $k=0$, then $g_k$ has three distinct real zeros.
If $k<0$, then $g_k$ has only one real zero.
The leading coefficient of $g_k$ depends on $k$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The equation $x^{3}=kx$ rearranges to $x(x^{2}-k)=0$, and a positive $k$ supplies two extra real square roots.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{k}(x)=x^{3}-kx$$

For $k=16$ the zeros are $-4$, $0$ and $4$.

$$g_{16}(-4)=-64+64$$

$$-64+64$$

$$g_{16}(-4)=0$$

Those three values are distinct. Direct checks

$$g_{16}(4)=64-64$$

$$g_{16}(4)=0$$

 and $g_{16}(0)=0$ complete the triple. The same pattern $0,\pm\sqrt{k}$ appears for every $k>0$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

At $k=0$ there is nothing left to take a square root of, and the cubic degenerates.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{0}(x)=x^{3}$$

$$g_{0}(1)=1\neq 0$$

while

$$g_{0}(0)=0$$

Distinct zeros ignore multiplicity: a squared factor still counts as one abscissa.

The graph of $x^{3}$ meets the axis only at the origin. Nearby, $g_{0}(2)=8\neq 0$ and $g_{0}(-2)=-8\neq 0$, so no extra real zeros hide off zero. One distinct real zero is not three.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

For $k<0$ write $k=-c$ with $c>0$, so the second factor is $x^{2}+c$, which has no real root.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{-4}(x)=x^{3}+4x$$

$$x^{3}+4x=x(x^{2}+4)$$

$$x^{2}+4\ge 4$$

The product $x(x^{2}+4)$ vanishes only at $x=0$. A check $g_{-4}(1)=1+4=5\neq 0$ shows there is no extra real root. A negative parameter therefore leaves a single real zero.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

A leading coefficient that depended on $k$ would have to sit in front of $x^{3}$, but that slot is occupied by the constant $1$.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{3}(x)=x^{3}-3x$$

$$g_{-3}(x)=x^{3}+3x$$

A nonzero coefficient of that highest power is what makes the degree exact.

Opposite values of $k$ change the linear term from $-3x$ to $+3x$ but leave the cubic term untouched. The leading coefficient does not depend on $k$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Oddness does not consult the parameter: both $x^{3}$ and $-kx$ flip sign when $x$ does.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{k}(-x)=-x^{3}+kx$$

$$g_{k}(-x)=-g_{k}(x)$$

$$g_{4}(-1)=-1+4$$

$$-1+4$$

$$g_{4}(-1)=3$$

and

$$-g_{4}(1)=-(1-4)$$

$$-(1-4)$$

$$-g_{4}(1)=3$$

Equivalently, every surviving power in the expansion must be odd.

The numerical check for $k=4$ matches, and the same identity holds for every other real $k$. The family is odd for every real $k$.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
The family is given explicitly, with the parameter sitting on a lower term, so the leading term never sees it.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g(x)=x \left(- k + x^{2}\right)$$

Factor $x(x^{2}-k)$ to read the root count from the sign of $k$.

Degree and the leading coefficient are read from the highest written power whose coefficient is not zero.

Parity is a coefficient reading: only odd powers make an odd map, only even powers make an even map.

title: Parameter α4: How Many Real Zeros?
context:
Let $g_k(x)=x^3-kx$ with real $k$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.

(Exam variant 93.)
statements: If $k>0$, then $g_k$ has three distinct real zeros.
If $k=0$, then $g_k$ has three distinct real zeros.
If $k<0$, then $g_k$ has only one real zero.
The leading coefficient of $g_k$ depends on $k$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Positive $k$ makes $x^{2}-k$ a difference of squares with two real roots, distinct from the root $x=0$ of the remaining factor.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{k}(x)=x(x-\sqrt{k})(x+\sqrt{k})$$

For $k=25$ this is $x(x-5)(x+5)$, with zeros $-5$, $0$ and $5$.

$$g_{25}(5)=125-125$$

$$125-125$$

$$g_{25}(5)=0$$

Distinct zeros ignore multiplicity: a squared factor still counts as one abscissa.

Three distinct real zeros, and the same counting holds for every $k>0$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The claim asks for three distinct zeros at $k=0$, but substituting that value leaves a triple root at a single point.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{0}(x)=x^{3}-0\cdot x$$

$$x^{3}-0\cdot x=x^{3}$$

$$g_{0}'(x)=3x^{2}$$

$$g_{0}'(0)=0$$

Distinct zeros ignore multiplicity: a squared factor still counts as one abscissa.

The graph of $x^{3}$ is flat at the origin and meets the axis only there. Distinct zeros require distinct numbers, so $k=0$ fails.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

If $k<0$ then $x^{2}-k>0$ for every real $x$, so the quadratic factor never contributes a real root.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{-16}(x)=x^{3}+16x$$

$$x^{3}+16x=x(x^{2}+16)$$

$$x^{2}+16\ge 16>0$$

The only real root of the product is $x=0$. A check $g_{-16}(1)=1+16=17\neq 0$ confirms no extra real zero. Every negative parameter leaves this single real zero.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The family is monic for every $k$: the coefficient of $x^{3}$ is written as $1$ and never mentioned as a function of $k$.

$$g_{k}(x)=x^{3}-kx$$

$$g_{8}(x)=x^{3}-8x$$

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

A nonzero coefficient of that highest power is what makes the degree exact.

The linear coefficient $-k$ does depend on the parameter, but the leading coefficient does not. The number in front of $x^{3}$ is constantly $1$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

A function built only from odd powers is odd, and $k$ merely scales the linear odd power.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{k}(-x)=-x^{3}+kx$$

$$g_{k}(-x)=-(x^{3}-kx)$$

$$-(x^{3}-kx)=-g_{k}(x)$$

The identity makes no restriction on $k$. In particular it holds at $k=0$, where $g_{0}(x)=x^{3}$ is the standard odd cube, and at $k=1$ one has

$$g_{1}(-2)=-6$$

$$g_{1}(-2)=-g_{1}(2)$$

. Every $g_{k}$ is odd.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
The family is given explicitly, with the parameter sitting on a lower term, so the leading term never sees it.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g(x)=x \left(- k + x^{2}\right)$$

Factor $x(x^{2}-k)$ to read the root count from the sign of $k$.

Degree and the leading coefficient are read from the highest written power whose coefficient is not zero.

Parity is a coefficient reading: only odd powers make an odd map, only even powers make an even map.

title: Parameter α5: How Many Real Zeros?
context:
Let $g_k(x)=x^3-kx$ with real $k$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.

(Exam variant 94.)
statements: If $k>0$, then $g_k$ has three distinct real zeros.
If $k=0$, then $g_k$ has three distinct real zeros.
If $k<0$, then $g_k$ has only one real zero.
The leading coefficient of $g_k$ depends on $k$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Factor $g_{k}$ and note that a positive $k$ gives two extra real square roots besides $x=0$.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{k}(x)=x(x^{2}-k)$$

$$
x=0,\qquad x = \pm\sqrt{k}
$$

Distinct zeros ignore multiplicity: a squared factor still counts as one abscissa.

For $k=36$ those zeros are $-6$, $0$ and $6$, three different real numbers. Direct checks

$$g_{36}(6)=216-216$$

$$g_{36}(6)=0$$

 and $g_{36}(0)=0$ complete the list. The same triple appears for every $k>0$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

At $k=0$ the two extra roots $\pm\sqrt{k}$ both collapse onto $0$, leaving a single axis point.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{0}(x)=x^{3}$$

$$x^{3}=0$$

$$x=0$$

Distinct zeros ignore multiplicity: a squared factor still counts as one abscissa.

Multiplicity three at the origin is still one distinct real zero. Nearby values $g_{0}(1)=1$ and $g_{0}(-1)=-1$ are nonzero, so no extra crossings hide off zero. The distinctness claimed for $k=0$ does not hold.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

A negative $k$ makes $x^{2}-k$ strictly positive, so it cannot vanish and cannot add a real root.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{-25}(x)=x^{3}+25x$$

$$x^{3}+25x=x(x^{2}+25)$$

$$x^{2}+25=0$$

has no real solution. The remaining factor $x$ gives the unique real zero $x=0$. A check $g_{-25}(1)=1+25=26\neq 0$ shows there is no extra real root. Only one real zero survives.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Compare the expanded form at two different parameters and read the cubic coefficient in each.

$$g_{6}(x)=x^{3}-6x$$

$$g_{0}(x)=x^{3}$$

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

Both start with $x^{3}$. The parameter controls only the coefficient of $x$, which drops out of the leading-term test: $g_{6}$ starts $x^{3}-6x$ while $g_{0}$ is the pure cube. The leading coefficient is $1$ for every $k$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Substitute $-x$ into the two-term rule and factor out a minus sign; $k$ never has to be specialised.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{k}(-x)=(-x)^{3}-k(-x)$$

$$g_{k}(-x)=-x^{3}+kx$$

$$g_{k}(-x)=-g_{k}(x)$$

Equivalently, every surviving power in the expansion must be odd.

The identity is an equality of polynomials in $x$ whose coefficients involve $k$ only as a spectator. It holds for every real $k$.

So the statement is True.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g(x)=x \left(- k + x^{2}\right)$$

Factor $x(x^{2}-k)$ to read the root count from the sign of $k$.

title: Parameter α6: How Many Real Zeros?
context:
Let $g_k(x)=x^3-kx$ with real $k$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.

(Exam variant 95.)
statements: If $k>0$, then $g_k$ has three distinct real zeros.
If $k=0$, then $g_k$ has three distinct real zeros.
If $k<0$, then $g_k$ has only one real zero.
The leading coefficient of $g_k$ depends on $k$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The real roots of $x^{3}=kx$ are $x=0$ and, when $k>0$, the two real square roots of $k$.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{k}(x)=x^{3}-kx$$

For $k=49$ one has

$$g_{49}(7)=343-343$$

$$g_{49}(7)=0$$

 and likewise $g_{49}(-7)=0$.

$$g_{49}(x)=x(x-7)(x+7)$$

Distinct zeros ignore multiplicity: a squared factor still counts as one abscissa.

The zeros $-7$, $0$ and $7$ are distinct. Every positive $k$ produces the same three-root pattern.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Put $k=0$ into $x^{3}-kx$ and count distinct solutions of $x^{3}=0$.

$$g_{0}(x)=x^{3}$$

$$g_{0}(-2)=-8\neq 0$$

Distinct zeros ignore multiplicity: a squared factor still counts as one abscissa.

Only $x=0$ solves the equation. Nearby, $g_{0}(1)=1$ and $g_{0}(2)=8$ are both nonzero, so the cube does not hide extra real roots. A triple root at the origin is not three distinct real zeros at $k=0$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

For $k<0$ the graph of $y=x^{3}$ meets the line $y=kx$ only at the origin, because a line of negative slope through the origin stays opposite in sign to $x^{3}$ off zero.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{-2}(x)=x^{3}+2x$$

$$x^{3}+2x=x(x^{2}+2)$$

$$x^{2}+2\ge 2>0$$

The quadratic factor never vanishes, so the only real zero is $x=0$. A negative $k$ leaves a single real zero.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The leading coefficient is read from the highest power, which is $x^{3}$ with coefficient $1$ in the given formula.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{k}(x)=x^{3}-kx$$

$$g_{11}(x)=x^{3}-11x$$

A nonzero coefficient of that highest power is what makes the degree exact.

Changing $11$ to any other $k$ never rescales $x^{3}$. The linear coefficient $-k$ does depend on the parameter, but that is not the leading coefficient. The leading coefficient is independent of $k$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Oddness can be checked on the factored form $x(x^{2}-k)$ as well as on the expanded form.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{k}(-x)=(-x)\bigl((-x)^{2}-k\bigr)$$

$$g_{k}(-x)=-x(x^{2}-k)$$

$$g_{k}(-x)=-g_{k}(x)$$

The factor $x^{2}-k$ is even in $x$, so the whole product is odd for every real $k$. A check at $k=3$:

$$g_{3}(-1)=-1+3$$

$$g_{3}(-1)=2$$

 and

$$-g_{3}(1)=-(1-3)$$

$$-g_{3}(1)=2$$

. The family is odd for every real $k$.

So the statement is True.

The family is given explicitly, with the parameter sitting on a lower term, so the leading term never sees it.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g(x)=x \left(- k + x^{2}\right)$$

Factor $x(x^{2}-k)$ to read the root count from the sign of $k$.

Degree and the leading coefficient are read from the highest written power whose coefficient is not zero.

Parity is a coefficient reading: only odd powers make an odd map, only even powers make an even map.

title: Hard Graph Read: Roots (-3, -1, 2)
context: The figure shows a cubic with leading coefficient $-1$ and zeros $-3$, $-1$ and $2$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The product of the zeros equals $0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The figure names a cubic with leading coefficient $-1$, so the far-right end is the end of $-x^{3}$.

$$p(x)=-(x+3)(x+1)(x-2)$$

$$p(x)=-x^{3}-2x^{2}+5x+6$$

For large positive $x$ the cubic term dominates and is negative.

$$\lim_{x\to+\infty}p(x)=-\infty$$

Odd degree with a negative lead therefore falls on the far right.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Substitute $x=-1$ into the named polynomial and simplify each power before combining.

$$p(x)=- x^{3} + 2 x^{2} - 5 x - 6$$

$$(-1)^{3}=-1$$

$$-(-1)=1$$

$$(-1)^{2}=1$$

$$2\cdot 1=2$$

$$(-1)^{1}=-1$$

$$-5\cdot (-1)=5$$

$$p(-1)=1+2+5-6$$

$$1+2=3$$

$$3+5=8$$

$$8-6=2$$

$$p(-1)=2$$

The computed height is $2$, which does not match the claimed $0$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Three distinct real zeros force two turning points, one in each interval between consecutive roots.

$$p'(x)=-3x^{2}-4x+5$$

$$(-4)^{2}-4(-3)(5)$$

$$p'(x)=16+60$$

$$16+60$$

$$p'(x)=76$$

The discriminant is positive, so $p'$ has two distinct real roots. Rolle's theorem already places them in $(-3,-1)$ and in $(-1,2)$. Two turning points occur.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

The intercept is the product of the factors at $x=0$, including the leading minus sign.

$$p(x)=-(x+3)(x+1)(x-2)$$

$$p(0)=-(3)(1)(-2)$$

$$-(3)(1)(-2)$$

$$p(0)=6$$

The height $6$ is positive, so the graph sits above the origin. Equivalently the expanded constant term of $-x^{3}-2x^{2}+5x+6$ is $+6$. A strict inequality only needs the sign of that intercept.

$$6>0$$

The intercept is positive.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The three zeros named on the figure are $-3$, $-1$ and $2$, none of which is $0$.

$$
(-3)\cdot(-1)\cdot 2 =6
$$

$$6=0$$

The product is $6$, not $0$. The intercept $p(0)=6$ being nonzero is the same information: $x=0$ is not a root. A product of zeros equals $0$ only when at least one zero is $0$, and none of $-3,-1,2$ is. The product of the zeros is not $0$.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
The figure prints no expanded formula, so the polynomial is recovered from the ticks: zeros, intercept, and the far-field sign.

$p(x)=-x^{3} + 2 x^{2} - 5 x - 6$.

A value is obtained by substituting the named number and collecting powers.

The factor theorem is a substitution: $x-r$ divides a polynomial if and only if the value at $r$ is zero.

title: Hard Graph Read: Roots (-2, 1, 4)
context: The figure shows a cubic with leading coefficient $-1$ and zeros $-2$, $1$ and $4$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The product of the zeros equals $0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Only the leading term of a cubic survives far to the right, and the stem already names that coefficient as $-1$.

$$p(x)=-(x+2)(x-1)(x-4)$$

$$p(x)=-x^{3}+3x^{2}+6x-8$$

Dividing by $x^{3}$ leaves $-1$ plus terms that vanish as $x\to+\infty$.

$$\lim_{x\to+\infty}p(x)=-\infty$$

The right-hand end therefore dives.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Substitute $x=1$ into the named polynomial and simplify each power before combining.

$$p(x)=- x^{3} - 3 x^{2} - 6 x + 8$$

$$1^{3}=1$$

$$-(1)=-1$$

$$1^{2}=1$$

$$-3\cdot 1=-3$$

$$1^{1}=1$$

$$-6\cdot 1=-6$$

$$p(1)=-1-3-6+8$$

$$-1-3=-4$$

$$-4-6=-10$$

$$-10+8=-2$$

$$p(1)=-2$$

The computed height is $-2$, which does not match the claimed $0$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Three distinct zeros force two turns. Rolle places a stationary point in each gap $(-2,1)$ and $(1,4)$, and a cubic derivative is quadratic, so those two are the full list.

$$p'(x)=-3x^{2}+6x+6$$

$$x^{2}-2x-2=0$$

$$x=1\pm\sqrt{3}$$

Both roots are real and distinct, so the graph has exactly two turning points.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The $y$-intercept is $p(0)$, read by multiplying the three linear factors at the origin.

$$p(0)=-(2)(-1)(-4)$$

$$-(2)(-1)(-4)$$

$$p(0)=-8$$

The comparison asked for is the strict inequality $-8>0$, which fails: the graph meets the vertical axis below the origin.

$$-8>0$$

The same number is the constant term of the expanded formula.

The intercept is negative rather than positive, and $-8>0$ fails.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Multiply the three marked zeros rather than guessing from a sketch of the intercept.

$$
(-2)\cdot 1\cdot 4 =-8
$$

Zero is not among $\{-2,1,4\}$, so the product cannot vanish. The same number is the constant term of $p(x)=-x^{3}+3x^{2}+6x-8$.

$$p(0)=-8$$

The product of the three zeros is $-8$, not $0$, so the claim fails.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
The figure prints no expanded formula, so the polynomial is recovered from the ticks: zeros, intercept, and the far-field sign.

$p(x)=-x^{3} - 3 x^{2} - 6 x + 8$.

A value is obtained by substituting the named number and collecting powers.

The factor theorem is a substitution: $x-r$ divides a polynomial if and only if the value at $r$ is zero.

title: Hard Graph Read: Roots (0, 1, 5)
context: The figure shows a cubic with leading coefficient $-1$ and zeros $0$, $1$ and $5$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The product of the zeros equals $0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

An odd power with a negative coefficient copies the sign of $-x$ at both infinities. The stem fixes the lead as $-1$ and the zeros as $0$, $1$ and $5$.

$$p(x)=-x(x-1)(x-5)$$

$$p(x)=-x^{3}+6x^{2}-5x$$

For large positive $x$ every factor is positive, and the overall minus sign sends the values to $-\infty$.

$$p(10)=-10\cdot 9\cdot 5$$

$$-10\cdot 9=-90$$

$$-90\cdot 5=-450$$

$$p(10)=-450$$

$$-10\cdot 9\cdot 5$$

The right end dives.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Evaluate the product of the three linear factors at the named input $x=1$.

$$p(x)=-x(x-1)(x-5)$$

$$p(1)=-1\cdot 0\cdot(-4)$$

$$-1\cdot 0=0$$

$$0\cdot -4=0$$

$$p(1)=0$$

$$-1\cdot 0\cdot(-4)$$

The factor $(x-1)$ is zero there, which is exactly the geometric meaning of a marked crossing at $x=1$. Expanding gives the same height.

$$-1+6=5$$

$$5-5=0$$

$$p(1)=0$$

The graph meets the axis at $x=1$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

A cubic with three distinct real zeros has two turning points: one in $(0,1)$ and one in $(1,5)$, by Rolle, and no more, because $p'$ is quadratic.

$$p'(x)=-3x^{2}+12x-5$$

$$x=2\pm\frac{\sqrt{21}}{3}$$

Those abscissas are about $0.47$ and $3.53$, both real. Two distinct stationary points sit on the graph.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The origin is itself a listed zero, so the height there is zero rather than a positive number.

$$p(x)=-x(x-1)(x-5)$$

$$p(0)=0$$

The claim is the strict inequality $p(0)>0$. Equality to zero fails that test: the factor $x$ already forces the intercept onto the axis.

$$0>0$$

The same number is the constant term of the expanded formula.

The intercept sits on the axis, not above it.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

A product of real numbers is zero precisely when at least one factor is zero. Read the three zeros off the stem.

$$
0\cdot 1\cdot 5 =0
$$

The factor $0$ already kills the product. Equivalently, $p$ has no constant term: every summand contains $x$.

$$p(x)=-x^{3}+6x^{2}-5x$$

The factor test is the substitution that asks whether the height vanishes at that abscissa.

The product of those three zeros is $0$.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
The figure prints no expanded formula, so the polynomial is recovered from the ticks: zeros, intercept, and the far-field sign.

$p(x)=-x \left(x^{2} - 6 x + 5\right)$.

A value is obtained by substituting the named number and collecting powers.

The factor theorem is a substitution: $x-r$ divides a polynomial if and only if the value at $r$ is zero.

title: Hard Graph Read: Roots (-1, 2, 3)
context: The figure shows a cubic with leading coefficient $-1$ and zeros $-1$, $2$ and $3$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The product of the zeros equals $0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Pull the cubic factor out of the expanded polynomial and read the remaining bracket as $x\to+\infty$.

$$p(x)=-(x+1)(x-2)(x-3)$$

$$p(x)=-x^{3}+4x^{2}-x-6$$

$$p(x)=x^{3}\left(-1+\frac{4}{x}-\frac{1}{x^{2}}-\frac{6}{x^{3}}\right)$$

The bracket tends to $-1$ while $x^{3}\to+\infty$, so the product tends to $-\infty$. The right end dives.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Substitute $x=2$ into the named polynomial and simplify each power before combining.

$$p(x)=- x^{3} - 4 x^{2} + x + 6$$

$$2^{3}=8$$

$$-(8)=-8$$

$$2^{2}=4$$

$$-4\cdot 4=-16$$

$$2^{1}=2$$

$$p(2)=-8-16+2+6$$

$$-8-16=-24$$

$$-24+2=-22$$

$$-22+6=-16$$

$$p(2)=-16$$

The computed height is $-16$, which does not match the claimed $0$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Count turning points from the derivative, not from a guess about how cubics look.

$$p'(x)=-3x^{2}+8x-1$$

The discriminant of that quadratic is $64-12=52>0$, so two distinct real roots.

$$x=\frac{4\pm\sqrt{13}}{3}$$

Those values lie near $0.13$ and $2.54$, one in each gap between consecutive zeros. Two turning points occur.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Substitute $x=0$ into the factored form to read the intercept.

$$p(0)=-(1)(-2)(-3)$$

$$-(1)(-2)(-3)$$

$$p(0)=-6$$

The claim $p(0)>0$ would need a positive height. Here the graph meets the vertical axis six units below the origin, matching the expanded constant term of $-x^{3}+4x^{2}-x-6$.

$$-6>0$$

The same number is the constant term of the expanded formula.

The intercept is negative, not positive.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Form the product of the three zeros named in the stem.

$$

title: Quartic Meets a Parabola Four Times

**A.** → True

Meetings of the two graphs are the real roots of $p-\ell=0$. Subtract the parabola from the quartic.

$$p(x)=x^{4} - 6 x^{2} + 5$$

**B.** → False

$$p(x)=x^{4} - 6 x^{2} + 5$$

$$p(x)-\ell(x)=x^{4}-6x^{2}+5-(x^{2}-1)$$

$$x^{4}-7x^{2}+6$$

The highest surviving power is $x^{4}$, so the difference is a quartic, not a cubic. A cubic would need that $x^{4}$ term to cancel, but $\ell$ only reaches degree $2$. The difference is not a cubic.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Evenness is the identity $p(-x)=p(x)$. Substitute $-x$ into the given quartic.

$$p(x)=x^{4}-6x^{2}+5$$

$$p(-x)=(-x)^{4}-6(-x)^{2}+5$$

$$p(-x)=x^{4}-6x^{2}+5$$

$$x^{4}-6x^{2}+5=p(x)$$

Only even powers appear, so reflecting the input changes nothing. Odd powers are absent, which is the coefficient test for evenness. The polynomial is even.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

A linear function has the shape $ax+b$, with highest power $x^{1}$. The second formula in the stem is a quadratic.

$$\ell(x)=x^{2}-1$$

The $x^{2}$ term is present with coefficient $1\neq 0$, so the graph of $\ell$ is a parabola, not a straight line.

$$\ell(-x)=x^{2}-1$$

$$x^{2}-1=\ell(x)$$

Evenness of $\ell$ is compatible with a quadratic, but it does not make $\ell$ linear. The function is not linear.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Evaluate both rules at the origin and compare the two numbers.

$$p(0)=5$$

$$\ell(0)=-1$$

$$5=-1$$

The same number is the constant term of the expanded formula.

The two heights are different: the quartic sits at $5$ while the parabola sits at $-1$. Equality would need the constant terms to match, and $5\neq -1$. Those two graphs do not meet at $x=0$, because $5\neq -1$.

title: Shared roots, parity, and nested degree
context: Two polynomials are given by $p(x)=x^{2} - 1$ and $q(x)=x^{3} - x$. Work with shared roots, parity, and nested highest powers. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Every real root of $p$ is also a root of $q$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A common linear factor is the shortest proof that a root of $p$ is a root of $q$, so factor both maps.

$$p(x)=(x-1)(x+1)$$

$$q(x)=x(x-1)(x+1)$$

$$x(x-1)(x+1)=x\,p(x)$$

$$
q(1)=0\qquad q(-1) = 0
$$

$$p(x)=x^{2}-1$$

The factor test succeeds only when that substitution returns zero.

Every real root of $p$ is already a root of $q$. Directly,

$$q(1)=q(-1)$$

$$q(1)=0$$

. Both real roots of $p$ lie among the roots of $q$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Oddness is the identity $q(-x)=-q(x)$, which holds as soon as only odd powers appear.

$$q(x)=x^{3}-x$$

$$q(-x)=-x^{3}+x$$

$$-x^{3}+x=-q(x)$$

$$q(-x)=(-x)^{3}-(-x)$$

$$q(-x)=-x^{3}+x$$

$$p(x)=x^{2}-1$$

There is no even-power term and no leftover constant. That is the definition of an odd function.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Evenness is the identity $p(-x)=p(x)$, which holds as soon as only even powers appear.

$$p(x)=x^{2}-1$$

$$p(-x)=(-x)^{2}-1$$

$$p(-x)=x^{2}-1$$

$$p(-x)=p(x)$$

Squaring kills the minus sign, and there is no odd-power term to survive the swap. Hence $p$ is even.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Nesting multiplies highest powers: the outer map $p$ has degree $2$ and the inner map $q$ has degree $3$.

$$p(q(x))=(x^{3}-x)^{2}-1$$

$$p(q(x))=x^{6}-2x^{4}+x^{2}-1$$

$$2\cdot 3$$

$$p(q(x))=6$$

$$p(x)=x^{2}-1$$

The leading term is $x^{6}$, and nothing cancels it because the leading coefficients are $1$ and $1$. The nested highest power is $x^{6}$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The other order multiplies the same two degrees: outer $3$ times inner $2$ is again $6$, not $5$.

$$q(p(x))=(x^{2}-1)^{3}-(x^{2}-1)$$

$$q(p(x))=x^{6}-3x^{4}+2x^{2}$$

$$3\cdot 2$$

$$q(p(x))=6$$

$$p(x)=x^{2}-1$$

The expansion begins with $x^{6}$. A drop to $x^{5}$ would have needed the leading coefficients to cancel, which they do not. The nested highest power is $x^{6}$, not $x^{5}$.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Both maps are already written.

$$
p(x) = x^{2}-1,\qquad q(x) = x^{3}-x
$$

Factor to linear pieces: $p=(x-1)(x+1)$ and $q=x\,p(x)$. Parity is a coefficient reading. Nesting multiplies highest powers rather than adding them.

title: The cubic family with a sliding gap
context: A one-parameter family is given by $g_{k}(x)=x^{3}-kx$. Decide oddness, repeated roots, distinct-zero counts, and stationary points as $k$ varies. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: For every real $k$, $g_{k}$ is an odd function of $x$.
If $k=1$, then $g_{k}$ has three distinct real zeros.
The value $k=0$ is exactly when $g_{k}$ has a repeated real root.
If $k=3$, the stationary points of $g_{k}$ are at $x=\pm 1$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Oddness is a coefficient reading: replacing $x$ by $-x$ must flip the whole formula, and that test does not see $k$ as soon as only odd powers appear.

$$g_{k}(x)=x^{3}-kx$$

$$g_{k}(-x)=-x^{3}+kx$$

$$-x^{3}+kx=-g_{k}(x)$$

$$g_{k}(-x)=(-x)^{3}-k(-x)$$

$$g_{k}(-x)=-x^{3}+kx$$

$$g_{k}(x)=x^{3}-kx$$

$$g_{k}(x)=x(x^{2}-k)$$

The identity holds for every real parameter. In particular $g_{k}(0)=0$ for every $k$. Oddness therefore holds for every real $k$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Three distinct real zeros appear when the quadratic factor $x^{2}-k$ has two distinct real roots besides the origin, so substitute the named parameter.

$$g_{1}(x)=x^{3}-x$$

$$x^{3}-x=x(x-1)(x+1)$$

$$x=-1,\ 0,\ 1$$

$$g_{k}(x)=x^{3}-kx$$

$$g_{k}(x)=x(x^{2}-k)$$

The factor test succeeds only when that substitution returns zero.

The three linear pieces are distinct. The zeros are $-1$, $0$ and $1$. Three distinct real zeros occur when $k=1$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

A repeated root occurs when $g_{k}$ and $g_{k}'$ share a root. Differentiate the family and compare.

$$g_{k}'(x)=3x^{2}-k$$

$$g_{0}(x)=x^{3}$$

A triple root at the origin is a repeated root.

$$g_{k}(x)=x^{3}-kx$$

$$g_{k}(x)=x(x^{2}-k)$$

The origin is always a root of $g_{k}$. It is also a root of $g_{k}'$ precisely when $k=0$, in which case $g_{0}(x)=x^{3}$ has a triple root at $0$. For $k\neq 0$ the nonzero roots $\pm\sqrt{k}$ (when they exist) are simple. The value $k=0$ is exactly the repeated-root case.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

A claimed root is a substitution, so put $k=4$ and $x=2$ into the family.

$$g_{4}(x)=x^{3}-4x$$

$$x^{3}-4x=x(x-2)(x+2)$$

$$g_{4}(2)=8-8$$

$$8-8$$

$$g_{4}(2)=0$$

$$g_{4}(x)=x(x-2)(x+2)$$

$$g_{k}(x)=x^{3}-kx$$

$$g_{k}(x)=x(x^{2}-k)$$

The factor $x-2$ is visible once $k=4$ is a perfect square. Directly, the two terms cancel. The named input is a root.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Stationary points solve $g_{k}'(x)=0$. For the named parameter that derivative is an even quadratic.

$$g_{3}'(x)=3x^{2}-3$$

$$3x^{2}-3=3(x^{2}-1)$$

$$x=\pm 1$$

$$g_{3}'(1)=g_{3}'(-1)$$

$$g_{3}'(1)=0$$

$$g_{k}(x)=x^{3}-kx$$

$$g_{k}(x)=x(x^{2}-k)$$

Compare the expanded formula at $-x$ with the original.

$$p(-x)\stackrel{?}{=}p(x)$$

Those are the two real solutions. The stationary abscissas of $g_{3}$ are $\pm 1$.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
The parameter sits on the linear term of an otherwise fixed cubic.

$$
g_{k}(x) = x^{3}-kx = x(x^{2}-k)
$$

Every member is odd, independently of $k$. Distinct zeros and stationary points then follow from the sign of $k$ and from $g_{k}'(x)=3x^{2}-k$.

title: Rebuild a touch-and-cross monic cubic
context: A monic cubic touches the axis at $x=1$ and crosses at $x=-2$. No expanded formula is given. Rebuild $p$ from that multiplicity pattern. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The rebuilt cubic has three distinct real zeros.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Monic normalisation plus the stated multiplicities pin the product down completely: a touch at $1$ and a simple crossing at $-2$.

$$p(x)=(x-1)^{2}(x+2)$$

$$p(x)=(x^{2}-2x+1)(x+2)$$

$$(x^{2}-2x+1)(x+2)=x^{3}-3x+2$$

Each factor is monic, and the square is forced by the touch at $x=1$.

Each linear factor is monic, and the square is forced by the touch. That product is exactly the displayed factorisation.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Distinct zeros ignore the exponent on a repeated factor. The rebuilt cubic vanishes only where a linear piece vanishes.

$$p(x)=(x-1)^{2}(x+2)$$

$$
x=1,\qquad x = -2
$$

$$
p(1)=0\qquad p(-2) = 0
$$

$$p(x)=(x-1)^{2}(x+2)$$

$$p(x)=x^{3}-3x+2$$

Those are two distinct abscissas, not three. Multiplicity total $3$ is not three distinct roots. Only two distinct real zeros occur.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

Only a root of multiplicity at least $2$ is automatically a root of the derivative. The crossing at $-2$ is simple, so differentiate and substitute.

$$p'(x)=3x^{2}-3$$

$$3x^{2}-3=3(x-1)(x+1)$$

$$p'(-2)=3\cdot 4-3$$

$$3\cdot 4-3=9\neq 0$$

$$p(x)=x^{3}-3x+2$$

$$p(x)=(x-1)^{2}(x+2)$$

$$p(x)=x^{3}-3x+2$$

The simple crossing is not stationary. The claimed vanishing of $p'$ at $-2$ does not occur.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Oddness requires $p(0)=0$ and $p(-x)=-p(x)$. Compute the intercept from the factors.

$$p(0)=(-1)^{2}(2)$$

$$(-1)^{2}(2)$$

$$p(0)=2$$

$$p(-x)=-x^{3}+3x+2$$

$$-p(x)=-x^{3}+3x-2$$

$$p(x)=(x-1)^{2}(x+2)$$

$$p(x)=x^{3}-3x+2$$

The factor test succeeds only when that substitution returns zero.

A nonzero constant term already kills oddness. The zero set $\{1,-2\}$ is not symmetric about the origin either. The rebuilt cubic is not odd.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Substitute $x=0$ into the named polynomial and simplify each power before combining.

$$p(x)=x^{3} - 3 x + 2$$

$$0^{3}=0$$

$$0^{1}=0$$

$$-3\cdot 0=0$$

$$p(0)=0+0+2$$

$$0+0=0$$

$$0+2=2$$

$$p(0)=2$$

The computed height is $2$, which does not match the claimed $-2$.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
A monic cubic is uniquely determined by a double root and a simple root: the touch supplies the square.

$$
p(x) = (x-1)^{2}(x+2) = x^{3}-3x+2
$$

Distinct zeros ignore multiplicity. A double root flattens $p'$; a simple crossing does not. The intercept is the product of the constant pieces.

title: Affine outer map around a difference of squares
context: Inner map $p(x)=x^{2} - 1$ feeds the outer affine map $q(x)=x - 2$. Compare $q(p(x))$ with $p(q(x))$ on degree, evaluation, and factors. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

An affine outer map has degree $1$, so it preserves the inner degree rather than raising it. Expand the nesting to confirm.

$$q(p(x))=(x^{2}-1)-2$$

$$(x^{2}-1)-2=x^{2}-3$$

$$1\cdot 2$$

$$(x^{2}-1)-2=2$$

$$p(x)=x^{2}-1$$

The highest power that appears is $x^{2}$. Nothing of degree $3$ can appear because $q$ is a line. The nested highest power is $x^{2}$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The other order is a quadratic outer map around an affine inner map, so the degrees multiply as $2\cdot 1=2$, not $3$.

$$p(q(x))=(x-2)^{2}-1$$

$$(x-2)^{2}-1=x^{2}-4x+3$$

$$p(x)=x^{2}-1$$

The expansion is quadratic. A cubic would have needed the inner map to contribute an $x^{2}$ of its own, which a line does not. The nested highest power is $x^{2}$, not $x^{3}$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

Nesting in opposite orders is a different composition, so evaluate both inside-out at the origin and compare.

$$q(p(0))=q(-1)$$

$$q(-1)=-3$$

$$p(q(0))=p(-2)$$

$$p(q(0))=4-1$$

$$p(q(0))=3$$

$$-3\neq 3$$

$$p(x)=x^{2}-1$$

The composite highest power is the product of the two individual highest powers.

The two numbers disagree. Equal nested degree does not make the two polynomials the same. Nesting does not commute here.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The factor theorem at $x=1$ asks whether $p(q(1))$ vanishes, equivalently whether $x-1$ appears after expanding the nesting.

$$p(q(x))=(x-2)^{2}-1$$

$$(x-2)^{2}-1=(x-1)(x-3)$$

$$p(q(1))=p(-1)$$

$$p(-1)=0$$

$$p(q(x))=(x-1)(x-3)$$

$$p(x)=x^{2}-1$$

The composite highest power is the product of the two individual highest powers.

The linear factor $x-1$ is visible in the factorisation, and the substitution confirms it. So $x-1$ divides the nesting.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Oddness requires only odd powers. The nesting $q(p(x))$ is a quadratic in $x^{2}$.

$$q(p(x))=x^{2}-3$$

$$q(p(-x))=x^{2}-3$$

$$q(p(-x))=q(p(x))$$

$$q(p(-x))\neq -q(p(x))$$

$$p(x)=x^{2}-1$$

The composite highest power is the product of the two individual highest powers.

Only even powers appear, so the nesting is even rather than odd. Even is the opposite of odd.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
The inner quadratic and the outer affine map are given explicitly.

$$
p(x) = x^{2}-1,\qquad q(x) = x-2
$$

Nesting multiplies degrees: $1\cdot 2=2$ and $2\cdot 1=2$. Expanding both orders gives different quadratics, so the compositions do not commute.

title: A squared factor and the derivative
context: A cubic arrives already factored as $p(x)=(x+1)^{2}(x-2)$. Use multiplicity, $p'$, the intercept, and parity — do not stop at expanding. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $p$ has exactly two distinct real zeros.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A root of multiplicity at least $2$ is automatically a root of the derivative, so read the squared factor and confirm by differentiating.

$$p(x)=(x+1)^{2}(x-2)$$

$$p'(x)=3x^{2}-3$$

$$3x^{2}-3=3(x-1)(x+1)$$

$$p'(-1)=0$$

$$p(x)=(x+1)^{2}(x-2)$$

$$p(x)=x^{3}-3x-2$$

The factor test succeeds only when that substitution returns zero.

The factor $x+1$ survives in $p'$, hence $p'(-1)=0$. The double root at $x=-1$ is stationary.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The root at $x=2$ is simple, so it need not flatten $p'$. Substitute into the derivative.

$$p'(x)=3x^{2}-3$$

$$p'(2)=12-3$$

$$12-3=9\neq 0$$

A simple root need not be stationary; only multiplicity at least $2$ forces $p'=0$.

The simple crossing is not a stationary point. The claimed vanishing of $p'$ at $2$ does not occur.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Distinct zeros ignore the exponent on $(x+1)^{2}$. The cubic vanishes only where a linear piece vanishes.

$$p(x)=(x+1)^{2}(x-2)$$

$$
x=-1,\qquad x = 2
$$

Multiplicity total $3$ is not three distinct roots.

$$p(x)=(x+1)^{2}(x-2)$$

$$p(x)=x^{3}-3x-2$$

Those are two distinct abscissas. Multiplicity total $3$ is not three distinct roots. Exactly two distinct real zeros occur.

title: Five independent small-integer traps

**B.** → True

Evenness is the identity $f(-x)=f(x)$, which holds as soon as only even powers appear.

$$f(x)=x^{4}+1$$

$$(-x)^{4}+1=f(x)$$

**C.** → True

$$
2\cdot 2 =4
$$

$$x^{4}-1$$

**D.** → True

**E.** → True

$$2(x-1)(x+1)+(x-1)^{2}=(x-1)(3x+1)$$

$$r'(1)=0$$

The factor $x-1$ survives in $r'$, so $r$ and $r'$ share the root $x=1$. A common real root therefore exists.

So the statement is True.

title: Remainders, mixed parity, nested power
context: Two polynomials are given by $f(x)=x^{3} - x$ and $g(x)=x^{2} - 4$. Use the remainder theorem, parity, and nested degree. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The remainder when $f$ is divided by $x-1$ is $0$.

The sum $f+g$ is an even function.
$f$ and $g$ share a common linear factor over the reals.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The remainder theorem says that the remainder on division by $x-1$ is the number $f(1)$, so substitute.

$$f(x)=x^{3}-x$$

$$f(x)=x(x-1)(x+1)$$

$$f(1)=1-1$$

$$f(1)=0$$

The factor $x-1$ is already visible, so the remainder is $0$. Equivalently, $f(1)=0$ is the remainder itself. The remainder is $0$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The same theorem for $g$ asks for $g(1)$, not for a guess from the shape of $f$.

$$g(x)=x^{2}-4$$

$$g(x)=(x-2)(x+2)$$

$$g(1)=1-4$$

$$g(1)=-3$$

$$-3\neq 0$$

That remainder is $-3$, not $0$. The factor $x-1$ does not divide $g$. The remainder is not $0$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

Even plus odd is even only if the odd summand vanishes. Add the two formulas and read the powers.

$$f(x)+g(x)=x^{3}+x^{2}-x-4$$

A surviving $x^{3}$ term is an odd power, which kills evenness.

$$f(x)=x^{3}-x$$

Compare the expanded formula at $-x$ with the negative of the original.

$$p(-x)\stackrel{?}{=}-p(x)$$

The $x^{3}$ term survives, so the sum is neither even nor odd. A surviving odd power kills evenness. The sum is not even.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Nesting multiplies highest powers: outer degree $3$ times inner degree $2$ is $6$.

$$
3\cdot 2 =6
$$

$$f(g(x))=(x^{2}-4)^{3}-(x^{2}-4)$$

$$f(g(x))=x^{6}-12x^{4}+47x^{2}-60$$

The leading term is $x^{6}$, and the leading coefficients $1$ and $1$ do not cancel. The nested highest power is $x^{6}$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

A common linear factor would have to appear in both factorisations.

$$f(x)=x(x-1)(x+1)$$

$$g(x)=(x-2)(x+2)$$

$$\{-1,0,1\}\cap\{-2,2\}=\emptyset$$

$$f(x)=x^{3}-x$$

The factor test succeeds only when that substitution returns zero.

The two lists of real linear factors are disjoint. No common real linear factor exists.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Both maps are given in expanded form.

$$
f(x) = x^{3}-x,\qquad g(x) = x^{2}-4
$$

The remainder on division by $x-1$ is the number $f(1)$ or $g(1)$. Parity is a coefficient reading. Nesting multiplies degrees: $3\cdot 2=6$.

title: A double root with a sliding companion
context: A monic cubic family is given by $p_{a}(x)=(x-1)^{2}(x-a)$. Track multiplicity, the derivative at the double root, and distinct-zero counts as $a$ moves. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: If $a=1$, then $p_{a}$ has a root of multiplicity $3$.
For every real $a$, $p_{a}$ is a monic cubic.
If $a=2$, then $p_{a}$ has three distinct real zeros.
If $a=0$, then $p_{a}$ is an odd function.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

When the sliding root lands on the double root, the two factors coalesce into a single triple factor.

$$p_{1}(x)=(x-1)^{2}(x-1)$$

$$(x-1)^{2}(x-1)=(x-1)^{3}$$

$$p_{1}(x)=(x-1)^{3}$$

Every factor is the same linear piece.

$$p_{a}(x)=(x-1)^{2}(x-a)$$

$$p_{a}(x)=x^{3}-(a+2)x^{2}+(2a+1)x-a$$

The factor test succeeds only when that substitution returns zero.

That is a root of multiplicity $3$ at $x=1$. The named parameter is exactly the coalescence case.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

A double root is a root of the derivative, independently of where the remaining simple root sits. For $a=2$ the double root at $1$ survives.

$$p_{2}(x)=(x-1)^{2}(x-2)$$

$$p_{2}'(x)=2(x-1)(x-2)+(x-1)^{2}$$

$$2(x-1)(x-2)+(x-1)^{2}=(x-1)(3x-5)$$

$$p_{2}'(1)=0$$

$$p_{a}(x)=(x-1)^{2}(x-a)$$

$$p_{a}(x)=x^{3}-(a+2)x^{2}+(2a+1)x-a$$

The factor $x-1$ survives in $p_{2}'$, hence $p_{2}'(1)=0$. The derivative vanishes there.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The parameter $a$ never touches the coefficient of $x^{3}$. Expand the leading term of the family.

$$p_{a}(x)=(x-1)^{2}(x-a)$$

$$(x-1)^{2}(x-a)=x^{3}-(a+2)x^{2}+\cdots$$

$$p_{a}(x)=x^{3}-(a+2)x^{2}+(2a+1)x-a$$

$$p_{a}(x)=(x-1)^{2}(x-a)$$

$$p_{a}(x)=x^{3}-(a+2)x^{2}+(2a+1)x-a$$

The leading coefficient is $1$ for every real $a$. Every member is a monic cubic.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Distinct zeros ignore multiplicity. For $a=2$ the factors are $(x-1)^{2}$ and $(x-2)$.

$$p_{2}(x)=(x-1)^{2}(x-2)$$

$$
x=1,\qquad x = 2
$$

Multiplicity at $x=1$ does not create a third distinct zero.

$$p_{a}(x)=(x-1)^{2}(x-a)$$

$$p_{a}(x)=x^{3}-(a+2)x^{2}+(2a+1)x-a$$

The factor test succeeds only when that substitution returns zero.

Those are two distinct abscissas, not three. Only two distinct real zeros occur.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Oddness requires only odd powers. The $a=0$ member still carries an $x^{2}$ term from the double root at $1$.

$$p_{0}(x)=x(x-1)^{2}$$

$$x(x-1)^{2}=x^{3}-2x^{2}+x$$

$$p_{0}(-x)=-x^{3}-2x^{2}-x$$

$$-p_{0}(x)=-x^{3}+2x^{2}-x$$

$$p_{a}(x)=(x-1)^{2}(x-a)$$

$$p_{a}(x)=x^{3}-(a+2)x^{2}+(2a+1)x-a$$

The $x^{2}$ term survives, so $p_{0}(-x)\neq -p_{0}(x)$. A zero intercept is not enough for oddness. So $p_{0}$ is not odd.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
The family keeps a double root at $x=1$ and lets a simple root slide with $a$.

$$
p_{a}(x) = (x-1)^{2}(x-a) = x^{3}-(a+2)x^{2}+(2a+1)x-a
$$

Every member is a monic cubic. Distinct zeros ignore multiplicity: one when $a=1$, two otherwise. An $x^{2}$ term destroys oddness.

title: Double at 2 and simple at −1
context: A monic cubic touches the axis at $x=2$ and crosses at $x=-1$. Rebuild $p$ from that multiplicity pattern, then test $p'$ and Vieta. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The multiplicity-weighted root sum equals $3$, matching the Vieta coefficient of $x^{2}$.
The rebuilt cubic has three distinct real zeros.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The unique monic cubic with a double root at $2$ and a simple root at $-1$ is the product of those monic linear factors.

$$p(x)=(x-2)^{2}(x+1)$$

$$p(x)=(x^{2}-4x+4)(x+1)$$

$$(x^{2}-4x+4)(x+1)=x^{3}-3x^{2}+4$$

$$p(x)=x^{3}-3x^{2}+4$$

$$p(x)=(x-2)^{2}(x+1)$$

$$p(x)=x^{3}-3x^{2}+4$$

The factor test succeeds only when that substitution returns zero.

Each factor is monic, and the square is forced by the touch. That product is the displayed factorisation.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

A double root is a root of the derivative. Differentiate the rebuilt cubic and substitute $x=2$.

$$p'(x)=3x^{2}-6x$$

$$3x^{2}-6x=3x(x-2)$$

$$p'(2)=0$$

The factor $x-2$ survives in $p'$, so the touch is flat.

$$p(x)=(x-2)^{2}(x+1)$$

$$p(x)=x^{3}-3x^{2}+4$$

The factor test succeeds only when that substitution returns zero.

The factor $x-2$ survives in $p'$, so the touch is flat. The derivative vanishes at the double root.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The root at $-1$ is simple, so it need not flatten $p'$. Differentiate and substitute.

$$p(x)=(x-2)^{2}(x+1)$$

$$p'(x)=3x^{2}-6x$$

$$p'(-1)=3+6$$

$$p'(-1)= 9\neq 0$$

The simple crossing is not a stationary point. The claimed inequality holds.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Vieta for a monic cubic reads the multiplicity-weighted root sum as minus the coefficient of $x^{2}$. Count the double root twice.

$$
2\cdot 2+(-1) =3
$$

$$p(x)=x^{3}-3x^{2}+4$$

Minus the $x^{2}$ coefficient is $-(-3)=3$, matching the weighted sum.

$$p(x)=(x-2)^{2}(x+1)$$

$$p(x)=x^{3}-3x^{2}+4$$

For a monic cubic the Vieta sum equals minus the coefficient of $x^{2}$.

$$r_{1}+r_{2}+r_{3}=-b$$

Minus the $x^{2}$ coefficient is $-(-3)=3$. The two readings agree. The multiplicity-weighted root sum equals $3$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Distinct abscissas ignore multiplicity. The rebuilt cubic vanishes only at $2$ and at $-1$.

$$p(x)=(x-2)^{2}(x+1)$$

$$
x=2,\qquad x = -1
$$

Multiplicity total $3$ is not three distinct roots.

$$p(x)=(x-2)^{2}(x+1)$$

$$p(x)=x^{3}-3x^{2}+4$$

Those are two distinct zeros, not three. Multiplicity total $3$ is not three distinct roots. Two distinct real zeros occur.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Monic normalisation plus the stated multiplicities pin the product down: a touch at $x=2$ and a simple crossing at $x=-1$.

$$
p(x) = (x-2)^{2}(x+1) = x^{3}-3x^{2}+4
$$

A double root flattens $p'$. Vieta reads the multiplicity-weighted root sum as minus the $x^{2}$ coefficient. Distinct zeros ignore multiplicity.

title: Two even maps nested both ways
context: Two even maps $p(x)=x^{2} - 1$ and $q(x)=x^{2} + 1$ are nested both ways. Track highest powers, sample values, real roots, and parity of the nestings. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Nesting multiplies highest powers. Each map has degree $2$, so both orders have degree $4$. Expand to confirm nothing cancels.

$$q(p(x))=(x^{2}-1)^{2}+1$$

$$(x^{2}-1)^{2}+1=x^{4}-2x^{2}+2$$

$$p(q(x))=(x^{2}+1)^{2}-1$$

$$(x^{2}+1)^{2}-1=x^{4}+2x^{2}$$

$$2\cdot 2$$

$$(x^{2}+1)^{2}-1=4$$

$$p(x)=x^{2}-1$$

Each expansion begins with $x^{4}$. Both nested highest powers are $x^{4}$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

A nested value is computed inside-out: evaluate $p$ at $0$, then feed that number into $q$.

$$p(0)=-1$$

$$q(p(0))=q(-1)$$

$$q(p(0))=1+1$$

$$q(p(0))=2$$

Expanding $q(p(x))=x^{4}-2x^{2}+2$ and substituting $x=0$ gives the same $2$.

$$p(x)=x^{2}-1$$

The composite highest power is the product of the two individual highest powers.

The nested value is $2$. Expanding $q(p(x))=x^{4}-2x^{2}+2$ and substituting $x=0$ gives the same $2$. The named value matches.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The other order at the same input is a different composition. Evaluate $q$ at $0$, then feed that number into $p$.

$$q(0)=1$$

$$p(q(0))=p(1)$$

$$p(q(0))=1-1$$

$$p(q(0))=0$$

$$p(q(x))=x^{4}+2x^{2}$$

At $x=0$ that expansion is $0$ as well.

$$p(x)=x^{2}-1$$

The nested value is $0$. Expanding $p(q(x))=x^{2}(x^{2}+2)$ displays a factor $x^{2}$, which vanishes at the origin. The named value matches.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

The outer map $q(u)=u^{2}+1$ is at least $1$ for every real $u$, so composing it with anything never hits height $0$.

$$q(p(x))=(x^{2}-1)^{2}+1\ge 1$$

$$(x^{2}-1)^{2}+1\ge 1>0$$

$$p(x)=x^{2}-1$$

Equivalently $x^{4}-2x^{2}+2=(x^{2}-1)^{2}+1$ has no real root. There is no real root.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

An even inner map makes any outer function of it even, and an even outer map composed with anything even in $x$ is even as well.

$$q(p(-x))=q(p(x))$$

$$p(q(-x))=p(q(x))$$

$$
q(p(-x))=q(p(x))\qquad p(q(-x)) = p(q(x))
$$

$$p(x)=x^{2}-1$$

The composite highest power is the product of the two individual highest powers.

Both expansions contain only even powers. Both nestings are even functions.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
Both maps are even quadratics.

$$
p(x) = x^{2}-1,\qquad q(x) = x^{2}+1
$$

Nesting multiplies degrees: $2\cdot 2=4$ in either order. Expanding gives different quartics. An even inner map makes any outer function of it even.

title: Three simple linear factors
context: A cubic is written $p(x)=(x-1)(x+1)(x-2)$. Test distinct zeros, $p'$ at a simple root, parity, Vieta, and the intercept. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $p$ has exactly three distinct real zeros.
By Vieta, the sum of the three roots is $0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Three distinct linear factors, each to the first power, give three distinct real zeros.

$$p(x)=(x-1)(x+1)(x-2)$$

$$x=-1,\ 1,\ 2$$

$$p(-1)=p(1)$$

$$p(-1)=p(2)$$

$$p(-1)=0$$

$$p(x)=(x-1)(x+1)(x-2)$$

$$p(x)=x^{3}-2x^{2}-x+2$$

None of the factors repeats, so none of the zeros is multiple. The count is three.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

A simple root need not flatten the derivative. Differentiate the product and substitute $x=1$.

$$p(x)=(x+1)(x-1)(x-2)$$

$$p'(x)=3x^{2}-2x-2$$

$$p'(1)=3-2-2$$

$$p'(1)= -1\neq 0$$

The crossing at $x=1$ is not stationary. The claimed vanishing of $p'$ fails.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

Oddness requires $p(0)=0$ and $p(-x)=-p(x)$. The intercept is the constant term of the expansion.

$$p(0)=2\neq 0$$

A nonzero intercept already kills oddness.

$$p(x)=(x-1)(x+1)(x-2)$$

$$p(x)=x^{3}-2x^{2}-x+2$$

A nonzero intercept kills oddness. The zeros $\{-1,1,2\}$ are not symmetric about the origin either. The cubic is not odd.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Vieta for a monic cubic reads the sum of the roots as minus the coefficient of $x^{2}$. Add the three simple roots.

$$-1+1=0$$

$$
0+2=2 =2
$$

$$p(x)=x^{3}-2x^{2}-x+2$$

$$-b=2\neq 0$$

$$p(x)=(x-1)(x+1)(x-2)$$

$$p(x)=x^{3}-2x^{2}-x+2$$

Minus the $x^{2}$ coefficient is $-(-2)=2$, not $0$. A vanishing $x^{2}$ term would have been needed for sum $0$. The root sum is $2$, not $0$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Substitute $x=0$ into the named polynomial and simplify each power before combining.

$$p(x)=x^{3} - 2 x^{2} - x + 2$$

$$0^{3}=0$$

$$0^{2}=0$$

$$-2\cdot 0=0$$

$$0^{1}=0$$

$$-(0)=0$$

$$p(0)=0+0+0+2$$

$$0+0=0$$

$$0+2=2$$

$$p(0)=2$$

The computed height is $2$, which does not match the claimed $0$.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
The cubic is already a product of three distinct monic linear factors.

$$
p(x) = (x-1)(x+1)(x-2) = x^{3}-2x^{2}-x+2
$$

Simple roots are crossings, not stationary points. Vieta reads the root sum as minus the $x^{2}$ coefficient. A nonzero intercept kills oddness.

title: Touch cubic on axes plus raw samples

title: Parity, shift, Vieta, and linear factors
context: Five standalone polynomial micro-scenarios — no shared formula across letters. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Translating $x^{3}-x$ upward by $2$ leaves exactly three real roots.
For $g(x)=x^{3}-4x$, the derivative $g'$ is an even function.
The quartic $x^{4}-5x^{2}+4$ factors into four real linear factors.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

A vertical shift preserves turning abscissas but can change the number of axis meetings. The unshifted cubic $x^{3}-x$ has local max/min of height $\pm 2/(3\sqrt{3})\approx\pm 0.38$, much smaller than the shift $2$.

$$q(x)=x^{3}-x+2$$

Shifting past both critical values of $x^{3}-x$ leaves a single real root.

Those tiny turning heights sit well below $2$, so only the left-hand tail still crosses the axis. The translated cubic keeps one real root, not three.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Evenness of a derivative is a coefficient reading. Differentiate $g(x)=x^{3}-4x$ and inspect the powers.

$$g'(x)=3x^{2}-4$$

$$g'(-x)=g'(x)$$

$$g'(-x)=3x^{2}-4$$

Compare the expanded formula at $-x$ with the original.

$$p(-x)\stackrel{?}{=}p(x)$$

Only even powers appear, so $g'$ is even. Differentiating an odd cubic always produces an even quadratic of this shape. The derivative is even.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Vieta for a monic cubic reads the sum of the roots, not an arbitrary integer. Add the three simple factors.

$$p(x)=(x+1)(x-1)(x-2)$$

$$-1+1=0$$

$$0+2=2$$

$$p(x)=2$$

$$-1+1+2=2\neq 8$$

The factor test succeeds only when that substitution returns zero.

For a monic cubic the Vieta sum equals minus the coefficient of $x^{2}$.

$$r_{1}+r_{2}+r_{3}=-b$$

Minus the $x^{2}$ coefficient of $x^{3}-2x^{2}-x+2$ is likewise $2$, not $8$. The claimed root sum is wrong.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Oddness is the identity $h(-x)=-h(x)$, and a zero intercept is the special case at $x=0$.

$$h(x)=-x^{3}+3x$$

$$h(-x)=x^{3}-3x$$

$$h(-x)=-h(x)$$

$$h(0)=0$$

Only odd powers appear, and the intercept vanishes. Both halves of the claim hold.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

A biquadratic is a quadratic in $x^{2}$, so factor it as such and then split each difference of squares.

$$x^{4}-5x^{2}+4=(x^{2}-1)(x^{2}-4)$$

$$(x-1)(x+1)(x-2)(x+2)$$

$$x=\pm 1,\ \pm 2$$

The factor test succeeds only when that substitution returns zero.

Four distinct real linear factors appear. The quartic factors completely over the reals.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
The five letters do not share a polynomial. Each micro-scenario is settled in its own letter: a vertical shift of $x^{3}-x$, the derivative of $x^{3}-4x$, a Vieta sum, oddness of $-x^{3}+3x$, and a biquadratic factorisation.

$$x^{3}-x+2\qquad 3x^{2}-4\qquad (x^{2}-1)(x^{2}-4)$$

A vertical shift preserves turning abscissas but can change the number of axis meetings.

title: Even quartic read from the axes
context: The figure shows a polynomial (solid) and a constant dashed companion. No algebraic formula is printed. Read the ticks: both ends, distinct axis meetings, intercept sign, oddness, and meetings with the dashed mark. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: As $x\to+\infty$ and as $x\to-\infty$, the solid graph tends to $+\infty$ in both directions.

End behaviour of an even-degree polynomial with positive lead is that both arms rise. Rebuild from the ticks: two touches at $\pm 1$ and a positive intercept force the monic even quartic

$$p(x)=(x-1)^{2}(x+1)^{2}$$

$$\lim_{|x|\to\infty}p(x)=+\infty$$

The leading term $x^{4}$ is positive for large $|x|$ on both sides. The solid graph tends to $+\infty$ in both directions.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

An axis meeting is a distinct abscissa of height zero. Each meeting here is a touch, at $x=\pm 1$.

$$p(x)=(x^{2}-1)^{2}$$

$$p(0)=1\neq 0$$

Both meetings are tangencies; the intercept $p(0)=1$ stays off the axis.

$$p(x)=(x^{2}-1)^{2}$$

$$p(x)=x^{4}-2x^{2}+1$$

The intercept is $+1$, so the curve does not return to height $0$ elsewhere in the window. Two distinct axis meetings (both tangencies) are visible.

So the statement is True.

Oddness is a half-turn about the origin. The figure is instead mirrored across the vertical axis, which is evenness.

$$p(0)=1\neq 0$$

Mirror symmetry across the vertical axis is evenness, the opposite of oddness.

$$p(x)=(x^{2}-1)^{2}$$

$$p(x)=x^{4}-2x^{2}+1$$

A positive intercept already kills oddness. Even is the opposite of odd. The solid graph is not odd.
